clue.text: Oft recited opening caught from Himalayan threnody on socket left out where he'd looted, perhaps

parts.words: Oft recited opening caught from Himalayan threnody
parts.note: surface reading: the first line of a mournful poem about the Himalayas that people love to declaim

parts.words: on socket left out where he'd looted, perhaps
parts.note: setter's reading: the idol in that poem has an empty eye socket, because the hero Mad Carew stole its green eye

explanation.surface: A much-quoted line from a sad Himalayan ballad about a plundered idol.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem is J. Milton Hayes's 'The Green Eye of the Yellow God', a staple of Edwardian recitations; Mad Carew steals the idol's eye, leaving an empty socket.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the famous first line of that monologue, the bit everyone quotes when parodying old music-hall recitals.

clue.text: Enzymic attempt on power twitch

parts.note: an attempt is a try
P is the physics symbol for power
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Someone attempts a muscle twitch while working on enzymes in a lab.
explanation.definitionFit: Tryptic describes something produced by or relating to trypsin, a digestive protein that breaks down other proteins.

clue.text: Mirror's objective seen though a glass darkly?

definitions.text: Mirror's objective seen though a glass darkly?

parts.note: surface reading: the aim of a mirror, or of the Daily Mirror newspaper; setter's reading: the Mirror's rival tabloid is the Sun, which it would love to see blotted out
a Bible phrase, but here literal: people watch this event through smoked or dark glass to protect their eyes

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding line about what a looking glass is for.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mirror and the Sun are rival British tabloid newspapers. The puzzle appeared weeks before the August 1999 total eclipse visible from Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: During this event the moon blots out our star, and viewers are told to look only through darkened filters.

clue.text: One casting out our possessions

parts.note: surface reading: someone throwing away our belongings in a clear-out
setter's reading: possessions by demons or evil spirits, which a priest drives out

explanation.surface: Someone ruthlessly decluttering the household and throwing out our things.
explanation.definitionFit: This person performs rites to drive evil spirits out of people they have taken hold of.

clue.text: Smith and Jones, say, follow-ing a nautical royal rising

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue something rising is read from the bottom upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: on a square-rigged ship the royal is a small sail set high on the mast

explanation.surface: Two people named Smith and Jones trail after a seafaring royal as it climbs.
explanation.walkthrough: Smith and Jones are the classic false names given when checking into a hotel incognito.
explanation.definitionFit: These common surnames are typical assumed names, used to hide a real identity.

clue.text: See 1 across
No hope, alas, for one born with a curious hatred of the novel

indicators.note: curious here means odd or peculiar, telling us the gathered letters come out in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I
B is the abbreviation for born in genealogies
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sad lament for a child born with a strange loathing of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The novel' looks like a book, but it means anything new.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek roots mean fear of new things, so the word names an aversion to anything unfamiliar or recent.

clue.text: Proportional representation

parts.note: surface reading: the electoral system where seats match vote share
setter's reading: a mathematical way of expressing how one quantity relates to another, such as 3:2

explanation.surface: The voting-reform slogan of electoral campaigners.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing two quantities as a pair like 3:2 shows their relative sizes, which is exactly how proportion is expressed.

clue.text: Trouble with one's nerve's needing creature comforts

parts.note: to be in hot water is to be in trouble
bottle is British slang for courage or nerve
the possessive ending supplies the letter as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a fix whose nerves need soothing with a few home comforts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing your bottle' is British slang for losing your nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubber containers filled from the kettle to warm a bed are a classic example of small physical luxuries at home.

clue.text: They are put out by opinion seekers

definitions.text: They are put out by opinion seekers

parts.note: surface reading: people annoyed or offended by pollsters
setter's reading: someone sounding out views extends tentative probes, like an insect's antennae

explanation.surface: Members of the public irritated by pollsters knocking on their door.
explanation.definitionFit: To test reactions discreetly is the idiom 'put out' these, borrowed from the antennae insects extend to sense their surroundings.

clue.text: See 1 across
Head in charge of the matter

parts.note: the head of something is its top
i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: Asking who leads the department dealing with this issue.
explanation.definitionFit: The subject under discussion is the thing a conversation or essay is about, its theme.

clue.text: Such children classed as having more than a whale of a time?

definitions.text: Such children classed as having more than a whale of a time?

parts.note: surface reading: youngsters sorted into classes, as in a classroom

parts.words: more than a whale of a time
parts.note: setter's reading: a group of whales is a school, so a whale's time spent in one suggests the period of life spent in classrooms

explanation.surface: Kids enjoying themselves enormously in their years at primary school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A whale of a time' is an idiom for great fun; whales swim in schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Children between roughly five and sixteen are legally required to attend lessons, and that span has this name.

clue.text: Board members only here? …

parts.note: surface reading: a sign restricting a room to company directors
setter's reading: the members are people who play on a checkered board with kings and pawns

explanation.surface: A notice on a boardroom door keeping out everyone but the directors.
explanation.definitionFit: A society of people meeting to play a strategy game on a sixty-four-square board fits members of the board.

clue.text: One seeking more than a pound of flesh in the main?

definitions.text: One seeking more than a pound of flesh in the main?

parts.words: seeking more than a pound of flesh
parts.note: surface reading: Shylock's demand in The Merchant of Venice, a moneylender exacting his due
setter's reading: the main is the open sea, home of a predatory fish

explanation.surface: A greedy creditor out for blood, or a predator hunting at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock demands a pound of flesh as security on a loan; 'the main' is a poetic word for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: An extortionate moneylender charges crushing interest and threatens violence, named after a predatory fish of the ocean.

clue.text: … members going on benders? On the contrary

definitions.text: members going on benders? On the contrary

parts.note: surface reading: club members, continuing from the previous clue, out on drinking sprees
setter's reading: reverse it, so benders (joints that bend) go on these members, as when someone kneels

explanation.surface: Following on from the chess club, its members go out on heavy drinking binges.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this to the previous clue. A bender is British slang for a drinking spree.
explanation.definitionFit: These leg joints are the parts that bend, and limbs are body members, so they are bending members.

clue.text: See 1 across
The ram's horn blown, not hot as yet

indicators.note: not says the following word's letter must be absent from what precedes it

parts.note: a shofar is the ram's horn trumpet blown in synagogue at Jewish festivals
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A ceremonial horn sounded, but not warmed up yet.
explanation.walkthrough: SHOFAR loses its H to leave SO FAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to this point in time is an idiom matching the adverb phrase meaning until now.

clue.text: English riders assembled in close formation

indicators.note: assembled means put together into a new arrangement, so these letters are rebuilt

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written

explanation.surface: English cavalry drawn up shoulder to shoulder for a charge.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes rows of soldiers or trees pressed tightly together with no gaps between.

clue.text: "He is brought ______ the slaughter" (Isaiah): (Absalom at slaying)

indicators.note: slaying means destroying, so the bracketed words are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A biblical quotation with a gap, paired with another biblical name meeting a violent end.
explanation.walkthrough: Absalom, King David's son, was killed by Joab, so 'slaying' suits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaiah 53:7 describes the suffering servant being led meekly to death like a young sheep to the butcher.

clue.text: See 1 across
Practices on the Whispering Glades fleet?

parts.note: re means on or concerning, as in business letters
Whispering Glades is the luxury cemetery in Evelyn Waugh's novel The Loved One; its fleet of vehicles carries coffins

explanation.surface: Asking about the vehicles of a fictional Californian funeral park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practices' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To go over a performance or speech in advance to prepare is what a performer does before the show.

clue.text: Whence 20,1across left from a holiday home

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: from here means taken away from, so the abbreviation for left is removed

parts.note: a villa is a rented holiday house abroad
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A saint who walked out of a holiday villa.
explanation.walkthrough: A VILLA loses one L. The answers at 20 and 1 across together name a Spanish mystic.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixteenth-century Carmelite nun and mystic is known by the name of her Castilian birthplace, so the town is where she came from.

clue.text: Has a peculiar interest, perhaps, in this mystic lady
Dull, but dry in the West!

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: Mae West was the Hollywood actress, so the West here is Mae
TT means teetotal, and a dry person drinks no alcohol

explanation.surface: A complaint that life out West is boring but at least alcohol-free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The West' looks like a region, but it is the film star Mae West.
explanation.definitionFit: A non-glossy finish on paint or photographs is described with this word, meaning lacking shine.

clue.text: Muse and friend fired thus?

parts.note: a muse is a source of creative stimulus
an ally is a friend; and simply joins the pieces

explanation.surface: A poet set alight by both their muse and a companion.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fired with enthusiasm by a muse has been stirred in a manner that stimulates creativity, the adverb's sense.

clue.text: Where the Irish dip their biscuits in lentil puree? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: in says one thing goes inside the other, here the dipping goes into the dish
this swaps which thing goes into which, so what was said to hold now goes inside

parts.note: to dunk is to dip biscuits in a drink
dal is the Indian dish of puréed lentils

explanation.surface: Asking where people in Ireland dip their biscuits into lentil mush.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the dipping goes into the lentils; the reversal puts the lentil dish inside the dipping instead.
explanation.definitionFit: This county town in Louth in the Republic of Ireland is a place where Irish people live.

clue.text: Bound to get a roasting?

parts.note: surface reading: certain to be scolded harshly
setter's reading: tied up, as a chicken is with string before going in the oven

explanation.surface: Someone certain to receive a severe telling-off.
explanation.definitionFit: Poultry has its wings and legs tied with string before cooking, and the word describes that tied-up state.
